An Illustrated Victorian Mystery · Book 2

The Cable

June 1887
The Wager Ledger
An illustrated edition · Complete original story

That June, London put on its flags the way a dowager puts on her diamonds: all of them at once, and slightly too early.

The Queen had reigned for fifty years, and the city meant to say so. Bunting ran from lamp-post to lamp-post down Regent Street. Plaster crowns sprouted over shopfronts that had never sold anything grander than gloves. Along Pall Mall, carpenters were building timber stands for the procession, tier on tier, so that the clubs seemed to be growing scaffolds the way old houses grow ivy. From the colonies came deputations in uniforms no one in Piccadilly could identify. From the East End came rumours, reported in the evening papers and then ignored, of men who would rather have had bread than bunting. And from every printing press in England came pictures of a small, stout widow in black, who had not much wanted any of it.

Mr. Phileas Fogg was fifty-five that year. His hair had gone from grey to white without consulting him, and he had given up taking the club stairs two at a time. He told himself this was a concession to dignity, not to his knees. In every other respect he was unchanged. He left 7 Savile Row at half past eleven, and he resented the Jubilee as much as a man of his temperament could resent anything. This was not on principle. It was because the stands in Pall Mall had closed the near pavement, and his walk to the Reform Club was now six hundred and twelve paces.

He had recorded the change in the green ledger without comment, the way an astronomer records a perturbation.

The forged telegram arrived on the fourteenth of June and very nearly ruined Mr. Ambrose Tolley.

Tolley was a member of comfortable size and uncomfortable nerves who had put more than was wise into the new gold reefs of the Transvaal. The year before, a man had kicked over a stone on a ridge called the Witwatersrand, and since then half the City had been trying to buy the stone. At ten minutes to three that afternoon, the club's hall porter handed Tolley a cable on the familiar buff form, apparently from his agent in Johannesburg: REEF PINCHED OUT NUMBER THREE SHAFT SELL WITHOUT DELAY. By half past three Tolley had sold, at a ruinous discount, to a buyer who had been waiting in Throgmorton Street with remarkable patience. By the following morning the shares had recovered, the agent in Johannesburg had cabled in bewilderment that number three shaft had never been better, and Tolley had taken to his bed.

The committee of the Reform Club did not care for its members being robbed in its own hall. Its chairman that year was Sir Hilary Venn, older now, and still red in the face. He remembered a thin young man and a snuffbox, and he sent to Baker Street.

The young man was not quite so young, and very much less obscure.

Over the past year the Yard had begun, grudgingly, to let his name reach the papers, and his friend the doctor had written up one of his cases with what Holmes considered an unforgivable taste for romance. The manuscript was now with a publisher of Christmas annuals. Between the two, he could no longer walk into a room without its noticing. He came into the Reform Club on the morning of the fifteenth and felt the change at once. Heads turned in the morning room. A member lowered his newspaper with the expression of a man who has seen a giraffe in Pall Mall. The hall porter, who in 1881 had taken his hat with no interest at all, now took it as if it might go off.

Holmes found this tiresome, and it was beginning to be useful.

He examined the telegram form. It was genuine Post Office stock, filled in with the even, characterless hand of a trained clerk. He examined the hall book and the porter. He asked what time the cable had come in. The porter said ten minutes to three. Then Holmes asked something the porter did not expect: whether the Cape cable had been working that afternoon at all.

The porter looked at him. Then, with the faint air of a man passing on a problem to the one person qualified to deal with it, he said, "You'd want to ask Mr. Fogg, sir."

"Why Mr. Fogg?"

"He wagers on it, sir. On when the Cape bulletin comes up on the board. Every day. To the minute."

"With whom?"

The porter considered this. "Himself, mostly, sir."

Mr. Fogg was in the reading room, in the chair that commanded the clock. Holmes knew him from across the room before he was halfway through the door. The white hair made no difference. Nor did the six years, or the green ledger lying on the arm of the chair. It was the stillness. In a room full of men turning pages and shifting in their seats and pretending not to look at the famous detective, one man was simply sitting, the way a stone sits in a stream. Holmes had last seen that quality from twenty paces behind, in a fog, and had written it down under the words Name unknown.

He felt something he would not have called pleasure. It was the small, clean click of a loose fact finding its drawer.

"Mr. Fogg."

Mr. Fogg looked up. There was no recognition in his face, then a little, then a precise amount.

"Venn's guest," he said.

"Six years ago. You have a good memory."

"I have a good ledger. You cost me a wager."

"I'm told," said Holmes, "that I cost you a good deal more than that."

Mr. Fogg did not answer this, which was answer enough. Around them the reading room had gone very quiet indeed. Several members were frankly listening, because the conversation had the air of a meeting between two notable persons. Only one of the two was aware of it, and that one was faintly enjoying it.

"I understand you're something of a celebrity now," said Mr. Fogg, in the tone in which another man might have said, I understand you have a cold.

"My friend the doctor has written an account of me. It's to appear in a Christmas annual, God help us both."

"I do not read Christmas annuals."

"Neither do I," said Holmes, with feeling. "I'd be glad of a different kind of reading. The porter tells me you keep a record of the Cape bulletin."

Mr. Fogg opened the green ledger without asking why. He did not care why. He found the page in four seconds, turned the book, and laid a finger beside an entry.

14 June. That the Cape bulletin will be posted by 3h 10m. Lost. No bulletin posted. Cable interrupted south of Aden, 1h 52m to 6h 20m. Restored per Eastern Telegraph Co. notice.

Holmes read it twice.

"Then no cable from Johannesburg reached London between two and six that afternoon," he said. "Not to the Post Office, and certainly not to the hall of this club at ten to three."

"None," said Mr. Fogg. "I lost a sovereign on it."

"Mr. Tolley lost rather more."

"Mr. Tolley," said Mr. Fogg, "ought to have known the cable was down. It was in the afternoon notices. Anyone can read them."

"Nobody does."

"No," Mr. Fogg agreed, without regret. He closed the ledger. "That is why I find them useful."

Holmes stood a moment longer than the business required. He could have asked a dozen things. He wanted to know where a man learns to time a submarine cable to the minute, and what kind of man turns the world's machinery into a private examination he sets himself every afternoon and nearly always passes. He asked none of them. Mr. Fogg had already turned back to his newspaper, and Holmes recognised, with a sensation close to fellow-feeling, a man who had said everything the occasion required and saw no reason to say more.

"May I have a copy of that entry?"

"I'll have it sent to Baker Street," said Mr. Fogg. "The ledger does not leave the house."

It was sent the next morning by the steward, who delivered it in person. He would not have trusted that particular errand to a boy.

He was nearer sixty than fifty now, round and pink, with a Jubilee rosette in his buttonhole that his master had not noticed and would not have approved. He walked up from Savile Row through streets so choked with stands and bunting and scaffolding that he had to go twice round by Portman Square. He arrived at the door of 221B mildly out of breath. On the step he found four small boys of uncertain ownership and unmistakable confidence.

"Mr. Holmes ain't to be disturbed," said the largest. "'Cept by us."

"I have a letter for Mr. Holmes from Mr. Fogg."

"Leave it with us, then."

The steward looked at them with professional interest. He had served masters on four continents, and he knew an organisation when he saw one.

"Tell me," he said, "how do you come from Savile Row to here with the Jubilee everywhere? I come by Portman Square and it is a desert of carpenters."

The boys exchanged looks of pure, delighted contempt.

"Portman Square!" said the largest. "Nobody goes by Portman Square. You cut through the mews behind Conduit Street, over the wall at the farrier's, through the back of the Bond Street dairy if you know the girl, and out by Wigmore Street. Eleven minutes, running."

"Nine," said a smaller one.

"Nine if you're Billy."

The steward considered this with deep respect. Then, because one does not take without giving, he told them how to get from Covent Garden to the river at low tide without once touching a street, by a route that went through two cellars and a church. He had found it in 1873 and never needed it since. The boys received it in reverent silence, like a relic.

"There's another thing," said the largest boy, lowering his voice now that they were colleagues. "Mr. Holmes has had us lookin' for a winder. Lit up. There's one in a top room in Gerrard Street been lit day and night three weeks now. Gas going full, nobody in. Landlady's fit to burst. Says when she finds the gentleman she'll have the bill out of his hide."

The steward was quiet for a moment.

"Three weeks," he said. "In an empty room."

"Burnin' all the time."

"Somebody will pay for it," said the steward, with the gravity of a man who knew exactly how much. "Believe me. Somebody always pays for it."

He gave them the letter. He also gave them sixpence each, which was more than he could afford. Then he walked back down to Savile Row by the mews behind Conduit Street, and he did it in fourteen minutes. He told no one, though he was rather proud of it.

The rest went quickly, as Holmes's cases tended to go once he had the shape of them.

The room in Gerrard Street had been let in May to a quiet young man who paid in advance and was never seen. The young man turned out to be a telegraph clerk dismissed from the St. Martin's-le-Grand office the previous winter. He had kept his skill, a supply of forms, and his grudge. He had taken the room to practise a Johannesburg operator's style of transcription from a bundle of old cables, bought from a man who should not have sold them. He had left the gas burning when he fled, hoping the light would suggest he was still at home and buy him a fortnight. It had bought him a fortnight, and then it had bought him the landlady.

The patient buyer in Throgmorton Street was a member of a rival club. He was asked to leave it, and he left. Tolley recovered his shares and his health, in that order. The Eastern Telegraph Company wrote a stiff letter to the Times about the confidentiality of its traffic. Nobody read that either.

Holmes's account to Sir Hilary ran to a single page. It did not mention Mr. Fogg, who would not have wished it to.

On the night of the twenty-first of June, all London was lit up.

Gas stars blazed over the clubhouses of Pall Mall, and crowns of coloured lamps over the shops in Regent Street. On the river, steamers strung with lanterns crept under bridges hung with more. The crowds were so thick in the Strand that people were carried along without touching the ground. The Queen had gone to the Abbey and come back, and had been, by every account including her own, very much moved and very tired. An empire that had not yet found out how large it was meant to become sat up late and congratulated itself.

In Savile Row, the windows of number seven showed a single lamp. Mr. Fogg had declined to illuminate, on the grounds that it would be visible.

He sat at his desk and wrote in the green ledger:

21 June. That the illuminations in Pall Mall will be extinguished by one o'clock.

He would not know until the morning, and he did not wait up for it. Before he closed the book, he turned back a week to the entry for the fourteenth: the cable that had not come, and the sovereign he had lost. In the margin, very small, he added a line. It was not a wager. Beside the gas jet billed and the cable cut and the Queen's fifty years, it was simply a record of the age.

Venn's guest. Holmes. Now famous. I do not entirely see why.

Two miles north, in the room above a lit and roaring Baker Street, Holmes took down his index and found the autumn of 1881. He looked for a moment at the line he had written then, The partner. Played the hand out. Returned his winnings without counting. Did not look at me once. Stride constant to a hair. Name unknown.

He struck out the last two words and wrote above them, in a neat small hand:

Fogg. Savile Row. Keeps the cable to the minute, for a sovereign, against himself. Why?

The doctor, coming in from the illuminations with his hat askew and his face pink with patriotic punch, asked what he was smiling at.

"A question," said Holmes, "that I am still not being paid to answer."
